newsitem.title: USA: Adv. Micro targets 30 pct of processor mkt.
newsitem.headline: Adv. Micro targets 30 pct of processor mkt.

text.p: Advanced Micro Devices Inc said it has in place the chip fabrication capacity to produce 30 million microprocessors a year and aims to grab 30 percent of the market for Windows compatible microprocessors.
Its immediate goal is to fill 22 percent of this market, Benjamin Anixter, vice president of external affairs, told the Robertson, Stephens & Co technology conference.

AMD is about to ship a new microprocessor, its K6, which will be the first chip from AMD in years to match Intel Corp microprocessors in performance. Anixter said AMD will ship "hundreds of thousands of units" of the K6 next quarter.
It has already shipped "significant" quantities of samples of the K6 to personal computer manufacturers, Anixter said.

With the K6, AMD has the chance to release a chip ahead of Intel, since Intel's comparable chip, the Klamath, is not expected to appear until late in the second quarter, with volume shipments later, officials and analysts say.

AMD recently completed an expensive expansion of its manufacturing capacity in Austin, Texas. Its microprocessors will be produced on state-of-the-art 0.35 micron processing technology with some on cutting edge 0.25 micron processing starting in the second quarter, he said.

But some analysts such as Roberton, Stephens' Dan Klesken say AMD sorely needs a good launch of the K6 to use up its capacity. "We believe a sucessful launch of the K6 is critical to AMD's goals of regaining market share and improving operating margins through better fab utilization," Klesken wrote in a recent report.
The 30 million units a year AMD plans to produce would compare with 10 million units a year of microprocessors that it has produced in recent years, Anixter said.
Anixter said AMD's other products of flash memory chips, programmable logic devices and semiconductor solutions for the communications market face good markets.
The flash memory market should grow from $2.6 billion in 1996 to $7 billion in the year 2000, he said.
"We are very bullish on flash," he said.
In communications, AMD sees good opportunity in the rapid deployment of telephone lines in developing countries. It supplies semiconductor gear that goes with telephone lines.
